This talk examines how medical practitioners and engineers can work together to create and protect meaningful MedTech innovations. Drawing on challenges relevant to medical devices, diagnostics, and AI-enabled tools, it explores how to distinguish an interesting research result from a potentially patentable invention, define inventive contributions, and coordinate publication with patent filing. It also discusses how early decisions about ownership, collaboration, and licensing can shape a technology’s future.

For people working across research and patient care, the session offers a practical way to think about intellectual property as part of the innovation process. The central question is: How can we turn shared expertise into a protected invention with a credible path to clinical use?

In the social sector, outcome-based finance has a seductive promise. Pay only when impact happens. No results, no money. Pay for Success. (Unless you are the Intermediary.)

Who could argue with that? I don't. For the right problem. Where the intervention is proven, the delivery is commoditised and the outcome is measurable, outcome contracts make sense. The causal chain is known. The only open question is execution: will this operator/NGO deliver, at this price/scale? That is deterministic risk. It can be priced. It can be contracted.

Now take an idea from the lab to the last mile. Will the science hold outside the lab? Can it be manufactured at a target price? Will a smallholder farmer or a district hospital actually adopt it? Will it survive the system it enters? That is not execution risk. That is discovery risk. And discovery cannot be contracted in advance.

An instrument that pays only on predetermined outcomes will quietly favour work where the answer is already known. Applied to innovation, it doesn't de-risk anything. It selects against the risk worth taking.

Ask one question of any "impact bond" or "outcome-based" structure: if the intervention fails, whose money is lost? Too often, the honest answer is nobody's. The investors sit behind guarantees and first-loss cushions. The outcome payer is the same philanthropic pool that would have written a grant anyway. The outcomes were chosen because they were easy to count, not because they mattered. Goodhart would recognise the pattern.

And the intermediaries? They take their cut upfront. Structuring fees. Advisory fees. Evaluation fees. Platform fees. All paid whether the impact arrives or not. Pay for success, it turns out, applies to everyone except the people designing the deal. The only party with no skin in the game is the one selling skin in the game :)

Meanwhile, the real risk has not gone anywhere. It still sits with the implementing organisation and, ultimately, the community, the people least able to say no.
Risk capital for innovation has to be honest about what it is buying: probability, not certainty. That does not mean less accountability. It means a different unit of accountability.

Judge the portfolio, not each bet. Fund in stages, against learning milestones that advance or kill an idea. Publish kill rates. Report failures as data, not embarrassment. Be explicit about which risk each rupee underwrites, and who loses it if things go wrong.

Uncertainty is not an exemption from evidence. It is a reason to measure differently.

So here is a modest proposal for the outcome-finance industry. Put intermediary fees on the same terms as everyone else. Paid on success. Clawed back on failure. Watch how quickly the enthusiasm for complex structures cools.

Impact bonds price execution risk. Innovation is discovery risk. Confusing the two doesn't de-risk anything. It just moves the risk to those with the least power to refuse it, while the fees move the other way.

Single-Use doesn’t have to mean Only Use.  

What if something designed to be thrown away can come back as something useful?  

At PadCare Labs, used sanitary pads are being transformed using 5D recycling technology. The process recovers the pulp and plastic from sanitary waste, putting these materials back into productive use. Alongside collection and reverse logistics, this creates a circular system where the waste is treated as a resource rather than something to simply throw away. 

But sustainability is not only about materials. It is also about people. 

PadCare also creates a safer and more formal working environment for people in the waste management workforce, helping move workers away from unsafe landfills and towards workplaces with greater safety and access to benefits such as health and employee insurance.  

It is a reminder that sustainable innovation can create value in more than one place – in everyday products we use, in systems we build and for the people who keep them running. 

From sanitary waste today to diapers, tissue paper and textile waste tomorrow, PadCare is expanding what can be part of the circular economy.

In B2C, the journey is often more direct, with factors such as price, convenience, brand, experience, and customer preference playing a major role.

For startups, understanding this difference can help you make better decisions around:

🔹 What motivates your customer to buy
🔹 Where you should reach them
🔹 How your sales journey should work
